title: Building a Personal Early-Warning System
hook: Most crises are preceded by small changes someone could have seen; an early-warning system is the habit of seeing them in yourself, and asking others to watch too.
why:
Every chapter in this part has described a body under strain: the stress posture, the shallow breath, the mask, the slowed walk of low mood, the climbing ladder of anger, the exhaustion of burnout, the extra drinks. Each has also made the same point. These states rarely arrive all at once. They build over days and weeks, through small changes in sleep, temper, appetite, contact with friends and the way a person holds and carries himself. By the time anyone names the problem, the run-up has usually been visible for a while.

This final chapter turns that knowledge into a system for your own life. It draws on research from the treatment of serious mental illness, where early-warning plans were first developed and tested, and is honest about what carries over to ordinary life and what does not. You will learn how crises announce themselves, how to find your own personal pattern of early signs, why acting early works better than acting late, how to write a simple traffic-light plan, how to recruit trusted people to watch for you, how to monitor without becoming obsessed, and when amber means it is time to see a doctor.

teach.p:
The modern study of early warning signs began with people at risk of relapse in serious mental illness. In 1989, Max Birchwood and colleagues developed an early signs scale for people with schizophrenia, completed both by the person and by a relative who knew them well. Changes such as anxiety, restlessness, poor sleep, withdrawal and irritability often appeared in the weeks before a relapse. In a small pilot study, the scale predicted relapse with an overall accuracy of about 79 per cent. And the relatives' reports mattered: in some people, who had lost insight into their own state as the relapse approached, observers saw changes that the person could not.

Similar patterns have been found in mood disorders. Research by Dominic Lam, Grace Wong and Pak Sham found that people with bipolar disorder could report the early signs of their episodes reliably, and that those who used practical coping strategies when the signs appeared were less likely to relapse. Early signs of depression were harder to catch than early signs of mania: about a quarter of the people they studied had difficulty detecting them.

These findings come from serious illness, and you should be careful about carrying them over. But the principle that most crises have a run-up is familiar from the earlier chapters of this part, from burnout to grief to heavy drinking, and it is the foundation of everything that follows.

The figure here walks slowly, head down. No single walk like this means anything. The same walk, every day for a fortnight, in someone who usually strides, is a change worth noticing, and the person walking is often the last to see it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if crises in mental health typically arrived without any preceding change. Early-signs studies find detectable run-ups in many people, though not in all, and the accuracy of prediction in the 1989 pilot came from a small sample.

teach.p:
Birchwood's later work introduced a useful phrase: the relapse signature. It is the particular set of early signs that a particular person shows, often in a similar order each time. One man's first sign is waking at four in the morning; another's is that he stops answering messages; a third starts picking fights with his brother. Generic lists of warning signs are a starting point, but your own signature is far more useful, because it is what you will actually see.

You find it by looking back. Choose a hard period in your past and work backwards from the point at which things were clearly bad. What changed in the month before that, and the month before that? Sleep, appetite, drinking, exercise, contact with friends, concentration, temper, how you dressed and groomed, how much you spoke, what you stopped enjoying. Then ask someone who knew you at the time what they noticed, because, as the early-signs research found, other people often see what you missed.

This is the reading method of this book turned on yourself. The chapters on baselines taught that a signal means something only against a person's normal. Your early-warning system is simply a written record of your own normal, and of the first ways in which you depart from it.

Most people find that their signature has an early stage, which is subtle and easy to dismiss, a middle stage, in which other people start to notice, and a late stage, in which everyone can see it. The aim is to act in the early stage. The figure here stands slumped, seen from the side. By this stage, most of the signature has already played out.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people's early signs varied randomly from one episode to the next. Clinical work suggests that signatures are often similar each time, but not always, which is why the plan should be reviewed after every hard period.

teach.h: Early action works better than late.
teach.p:
Noticing early signs helps only if it leads to action. The best evidence that it can comes from a trial published in 1999 by Alison Perry, Nicholas Tarrier, Richard Morriss and colleagues. People with bipolar disorder were taught, over a few hours in individual sessions, to identify their own early symptoms of relapse and to seek treatment quickly when they appeared. Compared with people who received usual care, they went much longer before a manic relapse, had fewer manic relapses, and did better in social life and employment over the following eighteen months.

The intervention did not reduce depressive relapses. The early signs of depression, as Lam's work also suggested, are harder to spot and harder to act on, perhaps because depression itself saps the energy and hope needed to act. This is worth knowing. A plan for low mood needs actions that are very small and very specific, and other people to help start them.

For each early sign in your signature, then, write an action you will take, and make it concrete. Not “look after myself”, but “go to bed by eleven, and no drink on weeknights”, “text Tom and arrange a walk”, or “book a doctor's appointment this week”. Early actions are usually simple: protect sleep, cut alcohol, keep contact with people, keep moving, reduce load where possible, and tell someone.

The figure here walks briskly, with purpose. Acting early is easier than acting late, because you still have the energy to act. The plan's job is to make the first step obvious, so that you do not have to decide what to do while the signs are already wearing you down.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if teaching people their early signs made no difference to outcomes. The 1999 trial found clear benefits for mania but not for depression, and it was conducted in bipolar disorder, so its results should not be assumed for every condition.

teach.h: Write it down: the traffic-light plan.
teach.p:
In 1997, Mary Ellen Copeland, working with people who had lived with mental illness, developed the Wellness Recovery Action Plan, known as WRAP. It asks a person to write down what they are like when they are well, what they do every day to stay well, what tends to trigger difficulty, their early warning signs, the signs that things are breaking down, and a crisis plan. In 2012, Judith Cook and colleagues reported a trial with 519 participants in which peer-led WRAP groups, meeting weekly for eight weeks, reduced psychiatric symptoms and increased hope and quality of life compared with usual services.

You do not need a course to use the idea. A simple version fits on one page, divided into three colours. Green describes you when you are well: how you sleep, eat, drink, move and spend time with people, and the daily habits that keep you there. Amber lists your early signs, from your signature, and beside each one the action you will take. Red lists the signs that you are in serious trouble, and exactly what happens then: who you call, which doctor or service, and the crisis line and emergency number for where you live, as in the safety plan described in the chapter on suicidal thoughts.

Write the plan when you are well, because that is when you have the judgment to write it. Keep it short, in your own words, and somewhere you will find it: on paper, in your phone, and with at least one other person.

The figure here takes notes. Ten minutes of writing on a good day can do more than hours of effort on a bad one, because on a bad day the plan does the thinking for you.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if written self-management plans made no difference. The WRAP trial found benefits, though its participants had serious mental illness, and applying the method to everyday stress is a reasonable extrapolation rather than something the trial tested.
teach.pullQuote: On a bad day, the plan does the thinking for you.

teach.p:
Because other people often see your early signs first, a good system includes them. Choose one or two people who see you regularly and whom you trust, such as a partner, a close friend, a sibling or a colleague. Show them your amber list. Agree what they will watch for, the words they will use if they see it, and what you will do when they say them. Agree, too, what they will not do, such as telling other people without asking you, unless they believe you are in danger.

The agreement matters because, without it, concern can feel like surveillance and is easily brushed off. The earlier chapter on the “I'm fine” mask described how many men close the door on questions about how they feel. A watcher with an agreed script can say, “You've missed football twice and you said you're not sleeping; that's on your amber list,” which is much harder to wave away than “Are you all right?” It also gives you words. Naming a sign from a list is easier than describing a mood.

Research on joint crisis plans shows why this must be done well. In 2004, Claire Henderson and colleagues found that among 160 people with psychosis or bipolar disorder, those who made a crisis plan with their care team were less likely to be admitted or treated compulsorily, 13 per cent against 27 per cent. But a larger trial, led by Graham Thornicroft and published in 2013, found no such reduction, though people with plans felt more respected. Later analysis suggested that many plans were generic and were not followed when a crisis came. A plan helps only when it is personal and actually used.

The figure here stands with two others. Your watchers are part of the system, not an audience for it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if involving others made early detection no better. Birchwood's observers helped where insight failed, but the crisis-plan trials show that involving others helps only when the plan is personal and followed.

teach.p:
It is tempting to think that more monitoring is always better: an app that asks about your mood five times a day, a watch that scores your sleep and stress. The evidence is more cautious. In the MONARCA trial, published in 2015, Maria Faurholt-Jepsen and colleagues gave people with bipolar disorder smartphones for daily self-monitoring with feedback from clinicians, and compared them with people who used ordinary phones. Over six months, daily monitoring had no significant effect on either depressive or manic symptoms, and the authors concluded that the approach needed careful evaluation before being used routinely.

Constant monitoring has a cost. As the chapter on interoception described, attending too closely to the body can feed worry, especially in people prone to anxiety. A mood score checked hourly becomes a new thing to be anxious about. And numbers from devices are prompts, not verdicts: a poor sleep score after a late night means you had a late night.

A better rhythm for most people is a brief, scheduled review. Once a week, at the same time, check your amber list against the past seven days. Is your sleep, drinking, contact, temper or energy different from green? One amber sign for a few days is ordinary life. Two or more for a couple of weeks is a signal to act on the plan. Then put the list away until next week.

The figure here walks while looking at a phone. Checking can become a habit that replaces living. The goal of a warning system is to free attention for your life, not to consume it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if frequent self-monitoring reliably improved outcomes. The MONARCA trial found no overall benefit from daily smartphone monitoring in bipolar disorder, though other monitoring approaches and other conditions may differ.

teach.h: When amber turns red, and when to see a doctor.
teach.p:
An early-warning system is not a substitute for help; it is a way of reaching help sooner. Write clear thresholds into your plan. Health services such as the NHS advise seeing a doctor if you have felt low, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy, most of the day, nearly every day, for more than two weeks. See a doctor, too, for sleep problems that persist for weeks, for drinking that is creeping up as a way of coping, and for any new or unexplained physical symptoms.

Some signs move straight to red. Any thoughts of suicide, or of not wanting to be here, mean using the red part of your plan today: talking to someone you trust, contacting your doctor or a crisis line, and, if you are in danger, the emergency services. The chapter on suicidal thoughts and the crisis resources in this app are there for that moment.

After every hard period, review the plan. Which signs came first this time? Did your watchers notice before you did? Which actions helped, and which did you skip? Update the list. Over the years, a plan revised after each episode becomes a precise map of how you, in particular, go under, and how you come back.

This chapter closes the part of the book on the inner world. Everything in it, from the stress posture to grief to burnout, has been about noticing the body under strain, in others and in yourself. A personal early-warning system is that knowledge made into a habit. The figure here stands open and steady: not a man who never struggles, but one who knows what his struggles look like when they start.
teach.disconfirm: The two-week threshold would be wrong for someone whose symptoms are severe or include thoughts of suicide; then the right time to get help is immediately, which is why such signs go straight to red.

poseGallery.doCaption: Acting at the first amber sign
poseGallery.annotation: Early signs are easier to act on than late ones, because you still have the energy to act. The plan's job is to make the first step automatic.
If you asked someone to watch for your signs, their concern is the system working. Thank them before you decide what it means.

poseGallery.annotation: Constant monitoring can feed worry. A short, scheduled review catches the trend without turning you into a subject under constant inspection.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Writing a plan in the middle of a crisis
poseGallery.annotation: A plan written at the bottom tends to be vague. Looking back together, while you are well, finds your own early signs.

caseStudy:
Ravi, fifty-two, had a long period of depression three years ago, after he was made redundant. Looking back with his doctor and his wife, Anjali, during his recovery, he found the order in which things had gone wrong. First he had started waking at four in the morning. Then he stopped reading, which he had always loved. Then he began drinking most evenings instead of on Fridays, stopped going to his chess club, and shaved only when he had to. By the time he admitted that something was wrong, all of it had been happening for two months.

He wrote a one-page plan. Green: walking the dog every morning, chess on Thursdays, seven hours' sleep, a drink on Fridays, Sunday calls with his daughter. Amber: four o'clock waking, no reading, weekday drinking, missed chess. Beside each, an action. Red: feeling like a burden or not wanting to be here, which meant calling his doctor the same day, with the crisis line written underneath. He gave copies to Anjali and to his friend Tom, and they agreed what Anjali would say if she saw amber.

Two years later, in the autumn his mother falls ill, Anjali notices that Ravi has missed chess twice and has been up before dawn most of the week. She says the agreed sentence: “Two things from your amber list this week. What do you want to do?” Ravi's first answer is that he is fine. Then he hears himself, and laughs, because “I'm fine” is on the list too.

He follows the plan. He stops the weekday drinking, goes back to chess, tells Tom, and books a doctor's appointment, where they agree some extra support for the months of his mother's illness. The dip lasts a few weeks instead of a season. When it has passed, Ravi updates the plan. This time, he noticed, the reading had stopped first.
observe: Notice the first thing that changes in you when a hard stretch begins: sleep, food, drink, temper, contact with friends or appearance.
Notice which people in your life comment on changes in you before you notice them yourself.
Notice how you respond when someone says you seem different, and whether your first answer is “I'm fine”.
Notice, in someone close to you, one small change that you would only have seen because you know their baseline.

drills.name: Look Back
steps: Choose a hard period in your past that you can think about without being overwhelmed.
Write down what your life looked like when you were well, just before it.
List the changes you remember, in the order you think they came.
Ask someone who knew you then what they noticed, and add it to the list.
Mark the two earliest signs: these are the first entries on your amber list.
variations: Do the exercise for a good period as well as a hard one, and note the first signs that things were going well.
Ask two different people what they noticed, and compare their lists with each other and with yours.

drills.name: Green, Amber, Red
steps: On one page, write Green: what you are like when well, and the daily habits that keep you there.
Write Amber: your early signs, with one concrete action beside each.
Write Red: the signs of serious trouble, who you will call, and the crisis line and emergency number where you live.
Read the plan aloud and cut anything you would not actually do.
Keep a copy on paper and in your phone, and give one to a person you trust.
variations: Write a version of the plan for a predictable hard time, such as an anniversary or a busy season at work.
Show the plan to your doctor or therapist, if you have one, and ask what they would add.

drills.name: Recruit a Watcher
steps: Choose one or two people who see you regularly and whom you trust.
Show them your amber list and explain what each sign looks like in you.
Agree the exact words they will use if they see amber, and what you will do then.
Agree what they will not do without asking you, unless they believe you are in danger.
Set a date, in three months, to review how it is working.
variations: Agree a code word for green as well as amber, so that your watcher can tell you when you seem back to yourself.
Write down what you will say, in the moment, if your first instinct on hearing the agreed words is to argue.

drills.name: Weekly Five Minutes
steps: Choose a fixed time each week, such as Sunday evening.
Read your amber list and compare each sign with the past seven days.
Write down any sign that has been present for several days.
If two or more signs have been present for two weeks, take the actions in your plan this week.
Put the list away until the next review, and do not check it daily.
variations: Try the review on a different day for a month and see whether a different time suits you better.
Add one line to the review: something that went well this week, to balance the attention on warning signs.

drills.name: After the Storm
steps: After any hard patch, set aside time once it has passed.
Write which signs came first this time, and in what order.
Note whether your watchers noticed before you did, and how you responded.
Note which actions helped and which you skipped.
Update your plan, and tell your watchers what has changed.
variations: Ask your watcher what it was like for them, and whether they would like anything about the arrangement to change.
Write a short note to your future self about what you learned this time, and keep it with the plan.

quiz.q: Is tracking your mood on your phone every day always helpful for people with mood problems?
options: Yes; daily tracking reliably prevents relapse in most of the people who use it regularly
Yes, as long as the app sends reminders several times during the day
Not necessarily; a trial of daily smartphone monitoring found no clear benefit
No; any kind of self-monitoring makes mood problems worse for everyone
quiz.explain: In the MONARCA trial, daily smartphone self-monitoring in bipolar disorder had no significant effect on depressive or manic symptoms. A brief, scheduled review is a better rhythm for most people than constant checking.

quiz.q: What did Birchwood and colleagues' 1989 early-signs work show about observers?
options: Relatives were too biased to notice any of the changes that mattered
Relatives' reports helped where people had lost insight into their own state
Observers were useful only when they were trained mental health clinicians
People always noticed their own early signs before their relatives did
quiz.explain: Relatives who completed the early signs scale sometimes saw changes that the person, losing insight as relapse approached, could not. This is the case for including trusted watchers in a personal plan.

quiz.q: In Perry and colleagues' 1999 trial, what happened when people with bipolar disorder learned to spot early signs of mania and seek help quickly?
options: Every kind of relapse stopped completely for the full eighteen months of the study
Nothing changed, because early signs of mania cannot be reliably spotted
Depressive relapses fell sharply, while manic relapses were unaffected
Manic relapses came later and less often, and work and social life improved
quiz.explain: The trial found a longer time to manic relapse, fewer manic relapses and better social functioning and employment. It did not reduce depressive relapses, whose early signs are harder to catch and act on.

quiz.q: Your friend asked you to watch for his early signs. He has missed football twice and says he is sleeping badly. What fits his plan best?
options: Use the words you agreed, name the signs, and ask him what he wants to do
Say nothing, since he will raise it himself if it becomes serious
Contact his doctor directly without mentioning any of it to him first
Tell the rest of the team, so that everyone can keep a close eye on him
quiz.explain: The point of an agreed script is that concern arrives as part of a plan he made, not as surveillance. Name the signs, use the agreed words and let him choose the next step, unless you believe he is in danger.

quiz.q: What does the contrast between the 2004 and 2013 trials of joint crisis plans suggest?
options: Crisis plans are harmful and are best never written down at all
Larger trials nearly always confirm the results of smaller ones
A plan helps only if it is personal and is actually used in a crisis
Plans work best when written without the person's own involvement
quiz.explain: The smaller 2004 trial found fewer compulsory admissions, but the larger 2013 trial did not, and many plans were generic and not followed. The lesson is that a plan must be personal and used, not merely filed.

quiz.q: For most of the past three weeks you have felt low, slept badly and lost interest in things you usually enjoy. What does this chapter suggest?
options: Wait another month to see whether it lifts on its own before doing anything
See a doctor now, because two weeks or more is a reason to get help
Increase your daily mood tracking until the numbers start to improve
Push harder at work, because keeping busy usually fixes low mood
quiz.explain: Health services advise seeing a doctor when low mood or loss of interest has lasted most days for more than two weeks. Any thoughts of suicide mean getting help immediately, without waiting.

quiz.q: In Cook and colleagues' 2012 trial, what happened in peer-led WRAP groups that met weekly for eight weeks?
options: Symptoms fell and hope and quality of life rose, compared with usual services
Nothing changed at all, because writing a plan has no effect on how people feel day to day
Symptoms rose sharply, because thinking about warning signs made everyone more anxious
Only participants who already had no symptoms at the start showed any improvement
quiz.explain: Peer-led WRAP groups reduced psychiatric symptoms and increased hope and quality of life compared with usual services. A personal plan, made with support, can change how people manage their own wellbeing.

quiz.q: Two of your amber signs, missing your Saturday run and not answering messages for days, have both been present for two weeks. What fits this chapter best?
options: Wait another month to be sure, since two weeks is far too short to mean anything
Ignore them, since you have been busy and busyness explains both of them
Take the amber actions written in your plan, and tell your watcher
Start checking your mood on your phone every hour until the signs go away
quiz.explain: Two or more amber signs for a couple of weeks is the signal the plan exists for. Acting early, with the small actions you chose in advance, works better than waiting until things are worse.

quiz.q: Someone says that early-warning plans are only useful for people with a diagnosed mental illness. What does this chapter say?
options: It is right, since only clinical relapses have a run-up that can be seen
Anyone can use one; stress, burnout and low mood usually have a run-up
It is right, and using a plan without a diagnosis can cause harm
It is wrong, but only for people who have had a crisis in the last year
quiz.explain: The research began with serious mental illness, but the idea applies to anyone. Most hard patches build through small changes that a personal plan can help you see sooner.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific hard period in your life, and look back at the weeks before it. What was the first thing that changed: sleep, drink, temper, contact with friends, appearance or something else? Who noticed, and what did they say? If someone had asked you to write an amber list a month before, what would have been on it? Write the two earliest signs, one action for each, and the name of one person you could ask to watch for them.
reflection.guidance: Looking back can be uncomfortable, so choose a period you can think about without being overwhelmed, and stop if it becomes too much. The goal is not a perfect history but two signs you can actually use. If you cannot remember any early signs, ask someone who knew you then; that is the first use of a watcher.

failureMode: The first failure is to wait until you are in crisis to plan, when you have the least energy and judgment to do it. The second is a generic plan, copied from a leaflet, that lists signs you have never had and actions you will never take; the crisis-plan trials suggest that plans work only when they are personal and used. The third is to recruit watchers without agreeing what they look for and what they say, so that concern feels like surveillance or is brushed off with “I'm fine”. The fourth is to monitor so constantly that the monitoring becomes a source of worry. The fifth is to ignore amber because it is not yet red. And the last is never to update the plan after a hard patch. Plan when well, keep it personal, share it, check weekly, act early and revise.

moreCases.title: The Saturday run she stopped going to
moreCases.scene:
Jo, forty-five, is a deputy head teacher. Two years ago she burned out badly in the spring term and was off work for six weeks. During her recovery, she and her friend Kate, who runs with her, looked back at how it had started. The first sign, they agreed, was that Jo had stopped coming to the Saturday morning parkrun, saying she had too much marking. Then she stopped answering Kate's messages on weekday evenings. Then she started having two glasses of wine every night rather than at weekends. By the time she went to her doctor, she was crying in the car every morning before school.

Jo wrote a one-page plan. Amber: missing parkrun two weeks running; not answering messages for three days; wine on a school night. Kate agreed to be her watcher, and they agreed that if Kate saw amber, she would say, "Amber, Jo," and Jo would book a meeting with her head teacher to talk about workload.

This October, in the run-up to a school inspection, Jo misses parkrun twice. On the second Saturday, Kate texts her a single word: "Amber."

Jo has also noticed, this term, that she has been reading emails in bed again, which she stopped doing after last time, and that she has cancelled lunch with her sister twice. Neither is on her amber list, and she wonders whether they should be.

Kate has been watching for this all term. She noticed the first missed run, and decided, as they had agreed, to wait for the second before saying anything, so that one busy Saturday would not set off an alarm.
moreCases.misread:
Jo's first reading of her own state, both times, was that she was simply busy, and that missing a run was a sensible choice when there was so much to do. Busyness is the most convincing disguise an early sign can wear.

And because the inspection was real and important, the busyness felt like the right priority, which is exactly what made it such an effective hiding place for the early signs.

Kate, on the other hand, read the same sign without the disguise, because she was outside the busyness and had agreed in advance what it meant.
moreCases.betterRead: Birchwood's idea of a personal signature fitted Jo closely: her first signs were small, specific and in a familiar order, starting with the Saturday run. A generic list of warning signs would never have included parkrun. Her plan worked because it was hers, because it named an action beside each sign, and because Kate had agreed in advance exactly what she would say. Perry and colleagues' trial showed that acting early on personal warning signs can delay or prevent relapse, and Jo's experience was a small, everyday version of the same thing. When Kate's text came, Jo's first instinct was to reply that she was fine, just busy. She did not. She booked the meeting with her head teacher on Monday, and they agreed to share the inspection preparation among three senior staff rather than leaving most of it to her. She went to parkrun the following Saturday, ran her slowest time in years, and texted Kate afterwards: "Green."

moreCases.title: The brother who did not know what to say
moreCases.scene:
Danny, thirty-eight, has watched his younger brother, Mark, go through two bad periods of depression in the past six years. Each time, Danny noticed things weeks before Mark did anything about them: Mark stopped coming to Sunday dinner at their mum's, stopped replying in the family group chat, and started posting late at night about not sleeping. Each time, Danny said nothing, because he did not want to interfere, and because he was not sure whether Mark would want him to.

This winter, Danny sees it starting again. Mark has missed two Sunday dinners. His messages have become one-word answers. Danny mentions it to their mum, who says Mark is a grown man and they should leave him alone.

On the third Sunday Mark does not come, Danny drives round to his flat. When Mark opens the door, Danny says, awkwardly, "Mum's worried you've gone quiet again," and Mark says he is fine, just busy, and does not ask him in.

Danny has also noticed that Mark has stopped going to the gym where they both train, and that when they did meet there last month, Mark left after twenty minutes, saying he was not feeling it.

Mark's posts have also changed. He used to share football clips and jokes; now he posts at two or three in the morning, about not being able to sleep, and deletes them by the time Danny wakes up. Danny has screenshots of two of them on his phone, and does not know what to do with them.
moreCases.misread:
Danny read his own role as an outsider who had no right to comment, and his mother read Mark's withdrawal as a grown man's choice. Mark, for his part, read Danny's awkward visit as his family checking up on him, which made it easier to close the door.

And because nobody had agreed anything, every member of the family was waiting for someone else to say something first.

And Danny's choice of words, "Mum's worried", put the concern on someone else, which made it easy for Mark to dismiss as his mother fussing.
moreCases.betterRead:
Watchers help most when the arrangement is agreed in advance, when the person being watched has chosen them, shown them what to look for, and decided what words they will hear and what they will do. Without an agreement, a well-meaning watcher has no script, and the person being watched has no reason to hear concern as anything but intrusion. Danny's visit, though awkward, was not wasted: it showed Mark that someone had noticed. The better route, which they took a few weeks later once Mark had seen his doctor, was to make the arrangement explicit. On a walk in the spring, Danny said that he had seen the signs both times before and never known whether to say anything, and asked whether Mark would like him to. Mark said yes, and they agreed: if Mark missed two Sunday dinners in a row, Danny would ring and say, "Two Sundays, mate," and Mark would book a doctor's appointment. The next winter, Danny rang. Mark booked it.

Danny also told their mum about the arrangement, with Mark's permission, so that she would know Danny was watching and could stop worrying quite so much on her own.

moreCases.title: The app that made him worse
moreCases.scene:
Lewis, twenty-nine, has had anxiety on and off since university. After a bad spell last year, he decides to get serious about catching it early. He downloads a mood-tracking app that prompts him five times a day, and buys a watch that scores his sleep, stress and recovery each morning. At first it feels empowering. Within a month, he is checking the watch twenty times a day. A poor sleep score in the morning makes him anxious for the rest of the day. A stress reading during a meeting makes him more stressed. He starts to dread the app's prompts, and to lie awake worrying about what his sleep score will be.

His partner, Femi, notices that he looks at his wrist constantly, even at dinner, and that his mood seems to rise and fall with the numbers.

When Lewis's anxiety gets worse rather than better, he tells his therapist that he has been doing everything right: he has never monitored himself so closely.

Femi has also noticed that Lewis wakes earlier than he needs to, picks up the watch first thing and studies the screen before he has said good morning. On mornings with a low score, he is quiet and tense all through breakfast.

Lewis has also started cancelling evenings out if his recovery score is low, telling Femi that his body needs rest. Femi has noticed that on those evenings Lewis does not rest at all. He sits on the sofa refreshing the app.
moreCases.misread:
Lewis read more monitoring as better monitoring, and took his rising anxiety as a sign that he needed to track even more closely. He did not see that the tracking had itself become one of the things making him anxious.

His therapist also noticed that Lewis described the scores in the language of judgment: a bad sleep, a failed day. The numbers had become verdicts on him.

Femi read it more accurately than Lewis did, because Femi was watching Lewis rather than the numbers.
moreCases.betterRead:
The MONARCA trial found that daily smartphone self-monitoring did not improve symptoms in people with bipolar disorder, and the chapter on interoception described how attending too closely to the body can feed worry, especially in people prone to anxiety. Lewis's constant checking had become a safety behaviour of the kind described in the chapter on anxiety: something that brought brief reassurance and kept the fear alive. Numbers from a device are prompts, not verdicts. His therapist suggested a different rhythm: a short written amber list of his own early signs, checked once a week on Sunday evening, and the watch taken off at night and left in a drawer. Lewis found the first fortnight hard, and kept reaching for his wrist. By the end of the month he was sleeping better, without knowing his score, and said that the weekly review told him more than the watch ever had.

He also told Femi about the change, and asked Femi to tell him if he started reaching for his wrist at dinner again. That made Femi his watcher, with an agreed sign.

moreCases.title: The plan written at the bottom
moreCases.scene:
Sean, forty-four, has heard about early-warning plans from a friend and decides to write one. He does it on a terrible night in January, after a row with his ex-wife about the children, when he cannot sleep and has been drinking. He downloads a template, fills it in quickly and copies most of the warning signs from a leaflet: feeling hopeless, losing interest, poor concentration, changes in appetite. For actions, he writes "exercise more", "eat healthily" and "think positively". He does not ask anyone to be a watcher. He saves it on his laptop and forgets about it.

Six months later, things are bad again. Sean remembers the plan, opens it and finds it useless. None of the signs are things he would actually notice in himself, and none of the actions are things he would actually do.

He mentions this to his doctor, who asks him a different question: what was the very first thing that changed, last time, before anyone could tell he was struggling?

Sean's ex-wife, who still sees him at handovers, has noticed the signs too, but she does not feel it is her place to say anything now, and Sean has not asked her to.

When the doctor asks his question, Sean realises that he does not know. He knows how he felt at the worst point, but he has no idea what came first, and nobody has ever asked him.
moreCases.misread:
Sean treated the plan as a form to fill in, and wrote it at the moment he was least able to think clearly about himself. He read generic signs as if they were his own, and generic advice as if it were a plan.

He also wrote it alone, so there was nobody to tell him that his real signs looked nothing like the leaflet's.

The leaflet's signs were not wrong for people in general. They were simply not his, and a plan made of other people's signs will not catch your own.
moreCases.betterRead:
The contrast between trials of joint crisis plans described in this chapter suggests that plans work when they are personal and actually used, and not when they are filled in for their own sake. A plan written in a crisis tends to be vague, because a person in crisis has little energy for the careful looking-back that finds their signature. Sean's better plan came from his doctor's question. On a calm afternoon, with his sister's help, he looked back and found his own early signs: stopping cooking and living on takeaways, missing his Wednesday evening with the children, and leaving the post unopened. Beside each he wrote an action he would really take: cook one proper meal, ring the children even if he could not see them, open the post with his sister on Sunday. His sister agreed to be his watcher. The new plan fitted on half a page, and he kept it on the fridge.

The first time one of the signs appeared, a pile of unopened post, his sister noticed it on a Sunday visit and they opened it together. It turned out to be the first useful thing the plan had ever done.

workedReading.title: Writing a plan together
workedReading.scene:
Ade, fifty, came through a long period of low mood last winter, with help from his doctor and a course of talking therapy. Now, in June, he feels well. His wife, Claire, suggests that they write an early-warning plan together while he is well, as his therapist recommended, so that next time they can both act sooner. Ade agrees, a little reluctantly. They sit at the kitchen table on a Sunday afternoon with a cup of tea and a blank sheet of paper divided into three colours.

Claire is aware that Ade did not want to think about last winter, and that he agreed mostly to please her. She decides to keep the session short, to stop if he wants to, and to make sure it ends with green, not red.

Claire has her own reasons too. Last winter she felt helpless for months, watching Ade slide and not knowing whether to say anything. She wants a plan as much for herself as for him.

steps.label: Choose a calm time
steps.text:
Claire chose the moment carefully: a Sunday afternoon, both rested and fed, Ade well and with nothing pressing. She knows from the chapter that plans written in a crisis tend to be vague and that a person in a low period has the least energy for this work. A plan written on a good day draws on a clear memory and a steadier mind.

She also suggests they do it at home rather than in a café, so that Ade can stop or walk away if it gets too much, and so that nobody overhears.

She also brings a printed copy of the chapter's three colours, so that the structure is there and they can spend their energy on remembering rather than on deciding how to lay it out.

steps.label: Look back together
steps.text:
They start with last winter. Ade remembers that the first thing he noticed was not sleeping past four. Claire remembers something earlier: that in October he had stopped playing the guitar in the evenings, and had started watching television instead without really watching it. Neither had thought much of it at the time. They write down everything they remember, in the order it came.

She also asks Ade's brother, with Ade's permission, what he remembers. His brother says that Ade had stopped coming for the Friday pint by November, which neither of them had connected with anything.

She also lets Ade lead. When he remembers something, she writes it down without adding her own view. When she remembers something he does not, she says it gently, as a question: "Do you remember when the guitar went quiet?"

steps.label: Mark the first two signs
steps.text:
From the list they pick the two earliest signs: stopping the guitar, and waking at four. These go at the top of amber, because they came weeks before anything that worried anyone. Claire notes that she noticed the guitar before Ade noticed the sleep, which is why her part in the plan matters.

She also notes that the guitar is a perfect early sign: specific, easy to see from outside, and something Ade does almost every evening when he is well. A good amber sign is one whose absence is obvious.

They also note what came later, in December: drinking more on weekdays, snapping at the children. Those are useful too, but they go lower on the list, because by the time they appear the slide is well under way.

steps.label: Write green and amber
steps.text:
For green, they describe Ade when he is well: guitar most evenings, walking to work, a pint with his brother on Fridays, seven hours' sleep. Beside each amber sign they write one action Ade would really take: if the guitar stops for a week, he will book a call with his therapist for a check-in; if he wakes at four for more than a week, he will see his doctor about his sleep.

They keep the actions small, so that Ade will actually take them. A check-in call is easy to book. A promise to exercise every day would be the kind of action that gets skipped.

Green also gets a line about people: the Friday pint with his brother and the Sunday call with his mother. Ade says that writing those down made him realise how much they keep him steady.

steps.label: Write red, with the numbers
steps.text:
For red, they write the signs that would mean serious trouble: not getting out of bed, stopping eating, talking about being a burden or not seeing the point, or any thoughts of suicide. Beside them they write exactly what happens: Claire calls the doctor that day, or the out-of-hours service, and if Ade talks about not wanting to be here, they use the crisis line and the safety steps in 2.13. They write down the numbers so that nobody has to search for them.

Writing red is the hardest part, and Claire notices Ade's shoulders rise. They take a short break, and finish it in five minutes, quickly, so that it is there if they need it and does not dominate the page.

They also add one line that is not a warning sign but a reminder, in Claire's handwriting: "Last time, it got better."

steps.label: Agree the words
steps.text:
Claire asks what she should say if she sees amber. Ade thinks about it and says he would rather she did not say "you're depressed again", which would make him defensive. They agree on "Guitar's been quiet, love", which is specific, gentle and about behaviour, and that when he hears it, Ade will take the amber action rather than argue. They also agree that Claire will not tell his family without asking him, unless she thinks he is in danger.

They also agree what Ade will say to Claire if she seems to be getting it wrong: "Not amber, love, just tired," which she promises to take seriously, and to look again in a few days.

Ade also asks Claire what she would like from him, as the watcher. She says that she would like him to tell her when he feels green again, so that she can stop watching for a while and just be his wife.

steps.label: Review and use it
steps.text:
They put a copy on the inside of a kitchen cupboard and one in Ade's phone, and set a reminder to review it in three months. In November, Claire notices that the guitar has been in its case for ten days. She says, "Guitar's been quiet, love." Ade's first impulse is to say he is just tired. Instead, he books the call with his therapist. They talk twice that month, and he gets through the winter without the long slide of the year before. In the spring, they update the plan together.

In the review, Ade adds one more amber sign: not shaving at weekends, which Claire noticed in November and which he had not realised he did.

Claire also notes, for herself, how different November felt. Last year she had watched and worried in silence for weeks. This year she said four words, and they both knew what to do.

moreFailures.title: Waiting until you are in crisis to plan
moreFailures.body:
The worst time to write an early-warning plan is when you need it most. In a crisis, energy is low, thinking is narrowed and memory is coloured by the present, so plans written then tend to be vague and generic, as Sean found. The best time is when you are well, ideally soon after a hard patch has passed, when you can still remember how it started and have the steadiness to look back. If you have never had a hard patch, you can still write a short plan from what you know about yourself: how you behave when you are stretched, and what usually helps.

It also helps to write the first draft quickly and improve it over time. A rough plan that exists is more useful than a perfect one that never gets written.

And if you are supporting someone else, the same applies: suggest a plan when they are well, not in the middle of a crisis, when it may feel like one more demand.

After a hard patch, set the date for writing or updating the plan before you feel completely well. Once life is back to normal, the memory of how it started fades quickly.

moreFailures.title: Copying a generic plan
moreFailures.body:
Leaflets and apps offer lists of warning signs, and they are a useful starting point. But a plan that lists signs you have never had, and actions you would never take, will not be used. The signs that matter are your own: the specific, small, early changes that you, or the people who know you, have actually seen before, such as stopping a hobby, missing a regular event or changing a daily habit. The actions that matter are concrete and realistic: a particular call, a particular appointment, a particular change to your week. A short personal plan beats a long generic one every time.

It also helps to include the people and places that keep you well in green, not only the habits. Green is not just a list of things you do; it is a description of a life that is working.

It also helps to keep the language your own. If you would never say "low mood" but would say "flat" or "not myself", write that. The plan should sound like you talking to yourself.

moreFailures.title: Recruiting watchers without an agreement
moreFailures.body:
A partner, friend or brother may see your early signs before you do. But without an agreement, they do not know whether you want them to say anything, what to say, or what will happen if they do, and you have no reason to hear their concern as anything but criticism. That is how watchers end up saying nothing, as Danny did for years, or saying it badly. Agree in advance what they will look for, the words they will use, what you will do when you hear them, and what they will not do without asking you. Then honour the agreement, especially when your first instinct is to say you are fine.

It also helps to thank your watcher when they speak up, even if you are not sure they were right. Being thanked makes it much easier for them to say it again next time.

It also helps to choose watchers who see different parts of your life. A partner may see sleep and temper; a colleague may see concentration and withdrawal at work. Two watchers with different views can catch what one would miss.

moreFailures.title: Monitoring too much
moreFailures.body:
More monitoring is not always better. Checking your mood, sleep or stress many times a day can turn a warning system into a source of worry, especially if you are prone to anxiety, and the evidence for intensive daily monitoring is mixed. Devices give numbers that look precise and often are not, and a poor score can spoil a day that was otherwise fine. A brief, scheduled review, once a week, against your own amber list, is enough for most people. Between reviews, put the list away and live your life.

It also helps to notice when the plan itself becomes a worry. If reviewing it makes you anxious, shorten it, review it less often, or ask your watcher to keep it for a while.

It also helps to build in green moments. A weekly review that only looks for problems can make life feel like a series of dangers. Noticing what went well keeps the system balanced.

questions.q: Isn't this only for people with a mental illness?
questions.a:
No. The research began with people at risk of relapse in serious mental illness, where early action can make a large difference, but the idea applies to anyone. Stress, burnout, low mood, heavy drinking and anger all tend to build gradually, through small changes that someone could have seen. A personal early-warning plan is simply a way of noticing your own run-up sooner and doing something about it. Many people with no diagnosis find it useful for the predictable hard patches in their lives: a demanding season at work, the anniversary of a loss, the winter months.

It also helps to include physical signs. Some people's earliest signs are bodily: headaches, a stiff neck, stomach trouble or catching every cold going. These belong on the amber list as much as changes in mood.

It may also help to think of it as the same kind of thing as knowing the warning light on a car's dashboard. Nobody needs a diagnosis to benefit from noticing early that something needs attention.

questions.q: What if my watcher gets it wrong?
questions.a:
Sometimes they will. A watcher may see an amber sign that has an ordinary explanation, such as missing football because of a family event. That is fine. The agreement is not that they will always be right, but that when they say the agreed words, you will take the agreed action, which should be small enough that doing it unnecessarily costs little. A call to a therapist or an appointment with a doctor that turns out not to be needed is a minor inconvenience. Review the arrangement together every few months, and adjust the signs or the words if they are not working.

It also helps to make the actions reversible. If the amber action is a check-in call, and the watcher was wrong, nothing is lost. If the amber action were something drastic, a false alarm would be costly, and people would stop using the plan.

questions.q: How do I ask someone to be my watcher?
questions.a:
Choose a calm moment, and keep it simple. You might say: "I've been working out the early signs I show when things start to go wrong, so I can catch it sooner. You see me more than most people. Would you be willing to tell me if you notice any of them?" Then show them your amber list, explain what each sign looks like in you, and agree the words and the action together. Make it clear that they are not responsible for fixing anything, only for saying what they see. Most people are glad to be asked, and many say that it is a relief to know what to do.

It also helps to choose someone who will actually see the signs. A close friend who lives far away may be less useful as a watcher than a colleague you see every day, for signs that show at work.

It also helps to give them permission to be wrong. "If you think you see it and you're not sure, say it anyway" makes the job far less frightening for the watcher.

questions.q: What if I have nobody to ask?
questions.a:
Then build the system with what you have. Your doctor or a therapist can help you write a plan, and some services offer ongoing check-ins. Peer support groups, including groups for people who have had particular difficulties, often include people who will notice and say something. A regular arrangement can be as simple as a weekly call or message with one person, even someone you are not especially close to. And your own weekly review is still valuable on its own. If you are isolated and struggling, the crisis lines in this app are there for you, too.

A pet can even help. Many people's first sign is that walks with the dog get shorter or stop, which is easy to notice and easy to put on a list.

It also helps to know that some workplaces, colleges and community groups offer buddy schemes or peer support that can play this role, and that asking about them is an ordinary thing to do.

questions.q: Should I use an app or a wearable?
questions.a:
They can help some people, especially as a reminder to do a weekly review or to notice patterns over months. But the evidence for intensive daily monitoring is mixed, as the MONARCA trial showed, and for people prone to anxiety, constant scores can become a new source of worry, as Lewis found. If you use one, set it up to support your plan rather than replace it: a weekly prompt rather than five a day, and numbers treated as prompts rather than verdicts. If you notice that you are checking more and feeling worse, put the device away for a while.

It may also help to notice what you use the device for. If it helps you sleep, move and connect more, it is supporting your plan. If it mostly gives you something new to worry about, it is not.

Some people find that a simple paper calendar, with a tick for each green habit, does the job better than any app, because it shows patterns over weeks without producing a score every morning.

questions.q: What if I see amber in someone who has not asked me to watch?
questions.a:
Then use the approach from the chapter on the I'm Fine mask: notice the change, choose a private, side-by-side moment, describe what you have seen as behaviour, ask how they are, and ask twice if it seems right. Respect their answer, and leave the door open. If they seem to be in serious trouble, or say anything that worries you about their safety, follow 2.13. Later, when things are calmer, you might ask whether they would like you to watch for those signs in future, which turns a one-off conversation into an arrangement.

It also helps to remember that the chapter's tools work together: noticing from this part, asking from the I'm Fine mask, and the safety steps from 2.13 if things are serious.

It also helps to remember that people often notice amber in someone else long before they notice it in themselves. That is exactly why watchers matter, and why a kind question from outside can be so useful.

watch.title: I'm Fine: Learning to Live With Depression
watch.notice: Jake Tyler describes the years he spent telling everyone he was fine. Listen for the early signs he missed in himself, and what finally made him notice.

reviewPrompt: This week, write your two earliest warning signs with one action for each, and tell one trusted person what they are.
